But we shall easily be disentangled from such scruples if we turn our mind to that dispensation of God which I have noted: that for that period in which he was delivering his Covenant to the Israelite people while it was still, in a sense, wrapped up, he willed to signify and figure both the grace of future and eternal happiness through earthly benefits, and the gravity of spiritual death through bodily punishments.

4. A second distinction between the Old and New Testaments is established in the figures <note>types or symbolic representations</note>: that the former, in the absence of the truth, displayed only an image and a shadow instead of the body; the latter exhibits the present truth and a solid body. And this is mentioned almost whenever the New Testament is opposed to the Old, though the treatment of it is more extensive in the Epistle to the Hebrews than anywhere else. There the Apostle <note>Paul</note> disputes against those who thought the observances of the Mosaic Law could not be abolished without dragging the ruin of the whole religion down with them. To refute this error, he takes up <margin>Psalm 110:4</margin> what had been predicted by the Prophet concerning the priesthood of Christ; for since an eternal priesthood is conferred upon him, it is certain that the priesthood in which successors were substituted for one another daily is abolished. Moreover, he proves that the institution of this new priest prevails because <margin>Hebrews 7:11, 19; 9:9; 10:1</margin> it is established by an oath. He adds afterward that in this transfer of the priesthood, a change of the Covenant is also brought about. And he confirms by reason that this was necessary, because such was the weakness of the Law that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to explain what that weakness was: namely, that it had external justifications of the flesh which could not make its worshippers perfect according to conscience, because through the sacrifices of cattle it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that it was a shadow of future goods, not the living image of the things themselves; and thus it had no other office except to be an introduction into the better hope which is exhibited in the Gospel.

Here we must see in what part the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical covenant, and the ministry of Christ with that of Moses. For if the comparison pertained to the substance of the promises, a great discord would exist between the two Testaments; but since the status of the question leads us elsewhere, we must aim there to find the truth. Let us, therefore, place in the middle the Covenant which he once sanctioned as eternal and never to perish. The fulfillment of that Covenant, from which it finally derives its established and ratified status, is Christ. While such confirmation was awaited, the Lord prescribed through Moses ceremonies which are, as it were, solemn symbols of confirmation. This came into contention: whether the ceremonies ordained in the Law ought to yield to Christ. These, although they were merely accidents of the covenant—or certainly additions and appendages, and (as the common people say) accessories—nevertheless, because they were the instruments of administering it, they bear the name of the "Covenant," just as is usually given to other Sacraments. Hence, in short, the Old Testament is called in this place the solemn method of confirming the covenant, comprised in ceremonies and sacrifices. Now, because nothing solid underlies it unless one passes further, the Apostle contends that it had to be antiquated and abrogated so that a place might be given to Christ, the surety and mediator of a better Testament, through whom eternal sanctification was once acquired for the elect, and transgressions which remained under the Law were obliterated. Or if you prefer, take it this way: the Old was the Lord's Testament which was delivered wrapped in the shadowy and ineffective observation of ceremonies; and therefore it was temporary, because it was as if in suspense until it could rest upon a firm and substantial confirmation. Then, however, it finally became new and eternal after it was consecrated and established by the blood of Christ. Hence the cup, which Christ reaches to the disciples in the Supper, he calls <margin>Matthew 26:28</margin> the cup of the New Testament in his blood: to signify that then the truth of God's Testament truly stands firm, through which it becomes new and eternal while being sealed with his blood.

5. From this it is clear in what sense the Apostle said that by the <term>pædagogia</term> <gloss>tutelage or schooling</gloss> of the Law, the Jews were led to <margin>Galatians 3:24; 4:1</margin> Christ before he himself was exhibited in the flesh. He confesses that they also were children and heirs of God, but who, because of their childhood, had to be held under the custody of a tutor. For it was fitting, while the sun of righteousness had not yet arisen, that there should be neither such a great flash of revelation nor such great clarity of understanding. Thus the Lord dispensed the light of his word to them in such a way that they saw it still at a distance and obscurely. Therefore Paul marks this thinness of understanding with the word "childhood," which the Lord willed to be exercised by the elements of this world and external little observances, as if by rules of childish discipline, until Christ should shine forth; through whom it was necessary for the knowledge of the faithful people to grow to maturity. Christ himself marked this distinction when he said that the Law and the <margin>Matthew 11:13</margin> Prophets were until John; from then on, the kingdom of God is preached. What did the Law and the Prophets provide to the men of their time? Surely they offered a taste of that wisdom which was one day to be manifested clearly, and they pointed to it gleaming from afar. But where Christ can be pointed to with a finger, the kingdom of God is unlocked. For in him are laid out <margin>Colossians 2:9</margin> all the treasures of wisdom and understanding, by which one penetrates almost to the very shrines of heaven.

<summary>Calvin explains the transition from the Old to the New Testament, defining the Law as a "shadow" or "tutor" that prepared the Israelites for the substantial truth found in Christ. He argues that while the substance of God's covenant is eternal, its outward administration changed from temporary ceremonies to the permanent mediation of Christ's blood.</summary>
<keywords>Old Testament, New Testament, Christ, Moses, Priesthood, Ceremonies, Covenant, Gospel, Tutelage, Shadow vs Substance</keywords>
